claims.text: The initial Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the initial alloy indicate dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The initial alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain.
Approximately 4 at.% Cr is added to the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
Cr addition induces precipitation of a complex C15 Laves phase during solidification or subsequent heat treatment.
Annealing above approximately 600 degrees Celsius but below the Laves-phase solvus is sufficient to trigger Laves-phase nucleation.
The Cr-induced C15 Laves phase has a volume fraction of approximately 4%.
The C15 Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected network along interdendritic boundaries.
The Laves-phase network coexists with a Cr-solute-supersaturated BCC matrix.
A reticulated Laves-phase network impedes crack extension by forcing crack deflection and branching.
Atomic-size mismatch associated with Cr solute causes lattice distortion and contraction of the BCC matrix.
Cr-induced lattice distortion produces solid-solution hardening.
BCC lattice contraction increases local hydrostatic stress at dendritic-interdendritic interfaces.
The increased interfacial stress promotes crack nucleation before the reticulated Laves phase can arrest the crack.
The stress-concentration effect of Cr-induced lattice contraction dominates Laves-network toughening, causing lower room-temperature fracture strain than in the Cr-free baseline.
XRD after Cr addition will show contraction of the BCC lattice parameter relative to the Cr-free baseline.
XRD after Cr addition will show C15 Laves-phase peaks.
The proposed fracture-strain decrease requires BCC lattice contraction greater than approximately 0.5% relative to the Cr-free baseline.
If the Laves phase forms as isolated particles rather than a reticulated network, fracture strain may not decrease.
The Laves-phase volume fraction and morphology are highly sensitive to cooling rate and thermal history.
